name: Bilal Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up for a nine o'clock lecture most days, then algorithms in the afternoon, and a lot of time in the library café arguing about assignments with my coursemate Priya. On Thursdays and Saturdays I work at a phone repair kiosk in the shopping centre. I live in a hall of residence, and my parents cover the room while I pay for everything else.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What led you to computer science?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've fixed phones since I was fifteen, first my cousins', then friends', and I started wondering how the software worked. My parents run a small grocery, so they like that the degree is something solid. I got in with average results and my plan is to just work steadily. I use AI tools now and then, mostly to explain a topic I didn't follow in lectures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that makes sense. It's a helpful tool, not a revolution. My friends would nod, and the kiosk customers would carry on asking if I can fix a cracked screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's reassuring, because computing stays a stable path. I'd still worry about how I'd afford the last years, since my parents' grocery has thin margins. If a supermarket chain moved in nearby, they'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Keep the kiosk shifts, keep using the AI for explanations only, and apply for a summer internship in year two. I'd also start putting a little aside, maybe fifteen pounds a week, in case the grocery has a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Steady. I think I'd be more worried about my assignment deadlines than about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the worry if things stayed this way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The family shop. My dad works twelve hours a day, and one bad winter or one big competitor could ruin it. If they struggled, I'd feel I should leave university and help in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd defer a year, probably, and I'd never tell my parents that's why, because they'd refuse to let me. It's what I'd do, though, if the shop was in real trouble.

say: I'd say it's a helpful **tool**, not a revolution, and carry on at the kiosk.
My friends would nod and move on.
think: Computing stays a **stable** path, which is reassuring.
My parents' grocery has thin margins, so my last years might be hard to afford.
do: Keep the kiosk shifts and apply for a summer **internship** in year two.
Put fifteen pounds a week aside in case the grocery has a bad year.
feel: I feel **steady**, more worried about deadlines than about AI.
S0.quote: I'd defer a year, probably, and I'd never tell my parents that's why, because they'd refuse to let me.
fieldNote: His real worry is his parents' **grocery**; he would defer a year to help but hide the reason.
Steady adaptability: uses AI for explanations, nothing beyond.
Money is the pressure point, not technology.

steps.text: Keep the Thursday and Saturday shifts at the phone repair kiosk
Apply for a summer internship in year two
Set aside fifteen pounds a week for the family shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change we all have to deal with, and some jobs will shrink. At the kiosk I'd tell people that repair work isn't going away soon. I'd stay out of online arguments, since neither side convinces anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think my degree is exposed. Writing code is one of the first things they name. Juniors are the ones who write the simple code, and simple code is what the cheap tools do first. I'd be competing with cheap tools for starter jobs, so I'd need to be better than basic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI but in a smarter way, to learn rather than copy. I'd ask the careers office which firms still hire juniors. And I'd push the phone repair side: it's hands-on and I could grow it into a small business if jobs got scarce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but not panicking. I'm more of a plodder: I keep going, and I check the facts first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the kiosk side look like if you grew it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do battery swaps and data recovery for people's old phones, maybe sell refurbished ones. My boss Dev says there's money in it if you're careful. I'd start small, with two hundred pounds of stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about around you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, my coursemate. She's brilliant at theory but she hates talking to people. If juniors are cut, those who can talk to clients will win. I'd tell her to join the debating society, even though she'd hate it.

say: I'd say it's a change we all have to deal with and some jobs will **shrink**.
At the kiosk I'd say repair work isn't going away soon.
think: My degree is **exposed**, since juniors write the simple code that AI does first.
I'd need to be better than basic to compete.
do: Use AI to **learn**, not copy, and ask the careers office who still hires juniors.
Grow the repair side with refurbished phones, starting with two hundred pounds of stock.
feel: I feel **tense** but not panicking, since I plod on and check facts first.
S1.quote: Juniors are the ones who write the simple code, and simple code is what the cheap tools do first.
fieldNote: He sees his degree as **exposed** and hedges with the hands-on phone repair business.
Concern for Priya shows his people-first outlook.

steps.text: Use AI to explain lectures, then redo the work himself
Ask the careers office which firms still hire juniors
Start selling refurbished phones with two hundred pounds of stock

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and we'll need new rules for money and work. I'd talk to my parents first, because they'd have no idea what it means. At the kiosk I'd be quiet and watch people lining up for repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my degree may not pay off. Two years is about when I'd be starting my third year, with code work going to machines. But phones are hands-on, so the kiosk work lasts longer, until the robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch my effort to the hands-on side, maybe turn the repair work into a full business. I'd ask my boss to teach me everything, including the money side. And I'd tell my parents to move their savings somewhere safe, not into the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I feel like the ground moved, and the loan is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be hardest about only having two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Choosing. I'd have to pick the course or the shop, and there's no time to try both. I hate making big decisions fast. I'd probably make a list and then change it ten times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I might leave my degree, and that I'd rather run something small and real than finish a certificate for work that's gone. My mum would say no. My dad would stay quiet, and then ask what I need.

say: I'd say we need new **rules** for money and work, and I'd talk to my parents first.
At the kiosk I'd be quiet and watch the queue.
think: My degree may not **pay off**, with code work going to machines by third year.
Phone repair is hands-on, so it lasts until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Turn the repair work into a full **business** and ask my boss to teach me the money side.
Tell my parents to move their savings somewhere safe.
feel: I feel **heavy**, as if the ground moved and the loan is still there.
S2.quote: I'd rather run something small and real than finish a certificate for work that's gone.
fieldNote: Under pressure he turns to the **hands-on** repair work and considers leaving his degree.
Hates fast decisions; two years takes away his slow, careful style.

steps.text: Ask his kiosk boss to teach him the business side of repairs
Consider leaving the degree to run the repair business
Tell his parents to keep their savings out of the shop
Cut everything except rent, food and phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but there's time to react, so let's be sensible. I'd talk it through with my parents and my boss. I'd say governments should publish a plan, since five years goes quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate in 2029, and thinking AI might already be taking starter jobs. But I'd have a few years to work on the repair side and a few years of coding. That would give me two options at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and run the repair work in parallel, growing it every summer. I'd apply for placements, and keep my AI use steady. And I'd save, because I might need money to start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned, but I think I could manage. It's a long enough run-up to avoid the worst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me do both things properly. With two years I'd have to pick, but with five years I can test the business on the side and keep the degree as insurance. It's less like jumping and more like climbing across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd keep the grocery, and my dad would ask me to help with the website. Robots on hands-on work come around 2034, so shops like theirs have more time, but the ordering and paperwork would change sooner. I'd set up the ordering system for them as a first test.

say: I'd say it's serious but there's **time**, and governments should publish a plan.
I'd talk it through with my parents and my boss.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 while thinking AI may already be taking **starter jobs**.
Running repairs beside the degree gives me two options.
do: Finish the degree and **grow** the repair business every summer.
Set up a simple ordering system for my parents' grocery as a first test.
feel: I feel **concerned** but able to manage with a long enough run-up.
S3.quote: With five years I can test the business on the side and keep the degree as insurance.
fieldNote: Five years lets him run **two tracks**, degree and repair business.
Brings in his parents' grocery, whose ordering and paperwork change sooner than the shelf work.

steps.text: Expand the repair business every summer holiday
Set up an online ordering system for his parents' grocery
Save toward start-up stock and a stall licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to adapt. I'd say stay curious and keep learning. I'd tell my parents to plan their shop around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'd be 28, which is plenty of time to try a few paths. A decade lets me get a degree, a first job, maybe a second job. I'd keep the repair skill because it's the kind of thing that always comes in handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, find a graduate job, and keep my kiosk skills as a side. I'd learn enough AI to be useful, not expert. And I'd help my parents modernise the shop, bit by bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I think. Maybe a bit bored, even, which is nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The not knowing. If ten years became six, I'd be annoyed with myself. But if I put a bit aside each month and keep two skills going, it feels covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing big. I'd stop being nervous about my grades, and I'd take the optional module on robotics since it looks interesting. I'd say yes to more things.

say: I'd say a decade is enough to **adapt** and people should stay curious.
I'd tell my parents to plan their shop around it.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28, with time to try a few **paths**.
Repair skill always comes in handy.
do: Finish the degree, take a graduate job and keep **kiosk** skills as a side.
Help my parents modernise the shop bit by bit.
feel: I feel **calm**, maybe a bit bored, which is nice.
S4.quote: If I put a bit aside each month and keep two skills going, it feels covered.
fieldNote: He is **calm** but keeps a slight edge because of his parents' shop.
Two skills (code and repair) is his insurance.
Would take a robotics module out of curiosity.

steps.text: Take a graduate job after the degree
Set up simple online ordering for his parents' grocery

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It forces a choice between the degree and the shop with no time to test either. What would help is a clear plan from government, advice for families with small businesses, and a way to pause a degree without losing my place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I worry about my parents more than myself. I can adapt, but their shop is their whole life. I'd like to know there's help for small shops, not just big firms.

headlineQuote: I worry about my parents more than myself. I can adapt, but their shop is their whole life.
portrait: Bilal is an **18-year-old** computer science student who fixes phones at a kiosk and whose parents run a small grocery.
He is centre-minded, steady and practical: he uses AI for **explanations** and checks the facts first.
His fallback is hands-on repair work, and he thinks in two tracks, degree and small business.
His mood moves from **uneasy** to alarmed at two years because the family shop is his real worry.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because it forces a choice between degree and the family shop.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **plan** from government, advice for small shops, and a way to pause a degree.
